Overall quality: moderate. The concept is clear, well-scoped, and targets an identifiable underserved segment, but the core value proposition rests on untested and somewhat shaky assumptions, and differentiation is thin.

Strengths: (1) The target user is specific (non-technical retirees), and the design choices (5-10 minute puzzles, plain-language hints, gradual progression toward realistic freelance tasks) follow logically from that segment's likely needs. (2) The founder mix covers tech, business, and pedagogy, and a working prototype with ~40 puzzles and early pilot users shows execution beyond ideation. (3) Positive early feedback ('enjoyed the puzzles, wanted more') is a legitimate, if weak, first signal.

Weaknesses: (1) The pain is asserted rather than evidenced. The plan says retirees feel bored and short on income, but offers no data, interview counts, or willingness-to-pay evidence. Boredom and income need are real but are generally addressed by many easier alternatives (volunteering, part-time retail, tutoring, gig work, existing skills). Coding is a high-effort path for this group, and the plan does not show why retirees would choose it. (2) The central promise, that a retiree can reach paid-freelance competence in a few months through 5-10 minute puzzles, is a large and unvalidated leap. Puzzle-based learning builds engagement, not marketable skill. The freelance market for beginners is crowded, price-compressed, and increasingly pressured by AI tools, so the income outcome may not materialize. There is no evidence that any learner has earned anything. (3) Pain and product are partly mismatched: the pleasure and mental-stimulation need is well served by puzzles, while the income need requires portfolios, client acquisition, trust, and job-platform navigation that the app does not address. The product risks falling between a brain-game and a vocational program without fully delivering either. (4) Differentiation is mostly positioning, not defensibility. Slower pace, plain language, and a senior focus are easily replicable by incumbents or by AI tutors that can already adapt explanations to any learner for free. The plan itself acknowledges this. (5) Early validation is limited to a small, friendly, self-selected pilot from one community center, with no engagement, retention, or completion metrics.

Uniqueness and compellingness: the niche is genuinely under-targeted, which gives some novelty, but the idea is an adaptation of existing coding-education formats rather than a fundamentally new approach. It is compelling emotionally and socially, less so commercially. The idea has merit as a learning-engagement product for older adults, but the income-generation framing needs real evidence (learner outcomes, retention, paid job conversions) before the problem-solution fit can be considered established.

Business plan text:

Codestable
Executive Summary: Codestable
Problem
Many retirees want to earn some extra money or keep their minds active after leaving their
careers. Fixed incomes do not always stretch as far as people expect, and a lot of retirees say
they feel bored or disconnected once they stop working. At the same time, there is a large
amount of freelance work available online, including website updates, spreadsheet cleanup and
simple automation. Most retirees who worked in fields like teaching, nursing, retail or office
administration do not have the technical background to do this kind of work. Existing coding
courses are mostly built for students and career changers in their twenties and thirties. They
move quickly, use a lot of jargon and assume the learner is comfortable with technology.
Retirees who try them often give up. We think this is a real problem for a growing group of
people, and we want to help.
Solution
Codestable is an app that teaches basic programming through short guided puzzles. Each puzzle
takes about five to ten minutes and teaches one small idea, such as how a list works or how to
repeat an action. The app gives hints at each step and explains mistakes in plain language
rather than technical terms. Users move through levels, and as they progress the puzzles start
to look more like real freelance tasks, for example fixing a broken web page or sorting a
spreadsheet. The idea is that a retiree can start with no experience and, after a few months of
regular use, have enough skill to take small paid jobs. We chose short puzzles because we
believe older learners prefer manageable sessions that fit into a daily routine and give a
quick feeling of success.
Market
There are over fifty million Americans aged sixty-five and older, and the number is growing
every year as the population ages. Many of them are comfortable using smartphones and tablets.
If even a small share of these people were interested in learning to code for part-time income,
the market would be very large. We estimate that if just two percent of retirees subscribed to
a product like ours, that would be a significant business. The freelance economy is also
growing, and more companies are comfortable hiring remote workers for small tasks. We believe
these trends together create a good opportunity for Codestable. Our initial focus will be
retirees in our region, who we can reach through community centers, libraries and senior
programs, before expanding nationally.
Business Model
Codestable will charge a monthly subscription. We are currently thinking of a price of around
twelve dollars per month, with a free trial period so people can try the app before paying. We
may also offer a discounted yearly plan. In the future we could add other revenue sources, such
as connecting graduates with freelance job platforms and taking a small fee, or partnering with
senior centers and retirement communities that could offer Codestable to their members as a
benefit. We have not yet tested these ideas, and we are still working out the right pricing and
how to bring in users at a low cost. Our main goal right now is to prove that retirees will use
the product regularly and find it valuable.
Competition
There are many coding education products on the market, including large online course platforms
and several popular apps for learning to program. These products are well funded and have many
users. However, they are generally designed for younger people and do not focus on retirees or
on freelance income. Codestable is different because it is built specifically for older adults
from non-technical backgrounds, with a slower pace, plainer language and a goal of helping
users earn money. We think this focus gives us an advantage, although we recognize that a

larger company could add similar features if they decided to target this group. We also compete
with free tutorials and videos that retirees could find on their own.
Team
Marcus Delacroix-Whitfield is a senior studying computer science at our university and built
the first prototype of the app. Priya Ramanathan-Ortiz is a junior studying business and is
responsible for user research and outreach. She spent a summer volunteering at a community
center, which gave her the idea for the project. Tobias Kellner is a junior studying education
and is designing the puzzle content and lesson structure. Together we cover technology,
business and teaching. None of us has run a company before, but we have worked well together on
class projects and are committed to the venture.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core concept, built a working prototype with an initial set of about
forty puzzles, and registered Codestable as an LLC. We also have a website that explains the
product. Recently we gave the prototype to our first external users, a small group of retirees
from a local community center, and early feedback has been encouraging. Several users said they
enjoyed the puzzles and wanted more. We have not yet charged anyone, so we have no revenue. Our
costs so far have been small and paid by the founders, mainly for legal registration and
website hosting. Over the next year we expect to spend money on app development, more puzzle
content, and marketing. If things go well, we hope to begin charging subscribers within about
nine months and reach a few thousand users in the first two years, though these numbers are
rough estimates.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to this competition to win funding and gain mentorship. We would use prize
money to hire a part-time developer, expand our puzzle library and run a larger pilot with more
retirees. We would also like advice from experienced entrepreneurs on pricing, how to reach our
customers affordably, and how to turn Codestable into a sustainable business. Feedback from
judges would be very valuable to us. We believe Codestable can help retirees learn new skills
and earn extra income, and we are excited to keep building it.
Question: Discuss the overall quality of the business concept or idea. Address whether the offering addresses a real and clearly identified pain or need in a unique and compelling way.
